newsitem.title: USA: Mercedes sees '97 U.S. sales over 100,000 units.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes sees '97 U.S. sales over 100,000 units.

text.p: German luxury car maker Mercedes-Benz AG expects to sell more than 100,000 vehicles in the United States for the first time in 1997, company executives said Sunday.

Mercedes, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, is expected to announce on Monday that it sold about 99,000 cars in the U.S. during 1996, beating the company's internal sales target of 85,000 units. Mercedes' 1995 U.S. sales totalled 76,752 cars.

Michael Bassermann, president of Mercedes-Benz North America Inc, told reporters that new products such as the SLK roadster, CLK coupe and M-Class sport/utility vehicle would boost sales in the second half of the year, but growth would be driven by continued strong sales of the company's core luxury sedans.
"The mainstay of our 1997 record will come from our core products -- C, E, S and SL-class models," he said.

The strong U.S. sales in 1996 helped push Mercedes-Benz' worldwide sales to about 645,000 vehicles, said Juergen Hubbert, management board member in charge of passenger cars. The total is about a 9.3 percent increase over the 590,200 units sold in 1995.

Mercedes officials unveiled the new CLK coupe at Detroit's North American International Auto Show. The coupe will go on sale in the autumn and is designed to compete with Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG's 3-Series coupes and Toyota Motor Corp's Lexus coupes.
Also unveiled was the chassis for the U.S.-built M-Class sport/utility vehicle, which also goes on sale this autumn.

In the U.S., the four-seat CLK, sized between the C and E class cars, will be priced in the same range as the SLK roadster, about $40,000, said Michael Jackson, head of sales and marketing for Mercedes-Benz North America.
Mercedes expects to sell about 40,000 CLK coupes worldwide in 1998, the car's first full year of production. About 10,000 of those will be earmarked for the U.S.

Daimler-Benz chairman Juergen Schrempp lauded the efforts of Mercedes management, but declined to comment on whether Mercedes chairman Helmut Werner would have a future role in the company's planned reorganisation.
Werner has opposed any threat to his unit's autonomy and many analysts believe he may be forced to leave Mercedes unless a deal is struck over the future of Daimler.
Asked if he was worried about possibly losing Werner to another company, Schrempp said: "I want to emphasise that he is a very good friend of mine."
Werner, who has regularly attended the Detroit auto show in the past, was not present on Sunday for the new product unveilings.
